desc:
Decide whether there are two different indices i and j with |i - j| ≤ indexDiff and |nums[i] - nums[j]| ≤ valueDiff. Return true if such a pair exists, otherwise false.

For example, nums = [1, 2, 3, 1], indexDiff = 3, valueDiff = 0 gives true (the two 1s), while nums = [1, 5, 9, 1, 5, 9], indexDiff = 2, valueDiff = 3 gives false.

Beware of values whose difference does not fit into a 32-bit integer; use 64-bit arithmetic if your language needs it.
hints: Checking every pair within distance indexDiff is O(n · indexDiff). Keep only the last indexDiff values in a data structure.
If you split the number line into buckets of width valueDiff + 1, two numbers in the same bucket always differ by at most valueDiff.

Keep a hash map bucket-id → value for the current window (one value per bucket is enough, since a second one would already have been a match). A new number can only match inside its own bucket or in the two neighbouring buckets; check those, then evict the number that has left the window.
editorial: Use bucket width w = valueDiff + 1 and the bucket id x // w (floor division, so negatives are placed correctly). Any two numbers sharing a bucket are within valueDiff of each other, so a bucket never holds more than one value of the current window without an answer already being found.

For each new x at index i: if its bucket exists, return true; if the left or right neighbour bucket holds a value within valueDiff of x, return true. Otherwise insert x and, once the window exceeds indexDiff elements, delete the bucket of nums[i - indexDiff]. Each step is O(1), so the total is O(n) time with O(min(n, indexDiff)) space. A sorted set gives O(n log n) instead.
